source_title: The We Company (WeWork) Form S-1 Registration Statement
publisher_issuer: The We Company (WeWork), filed with U.S. SEC (EDGAR CIK 0001533523)
company_context: The We Company (WeWork) is a flexible-office / coworking real-estate operator that filed its S-1 on August 14, 2019 ahead of a planned IPO. The filing disclosed large losses, governance and related-party concerns involving co-founder/CEO Adam Neumann, and a dual-class structure; investor backlash led WeWork to withdraw the IPO and Neumann to step down.
evidence_summary: WeWork showed rapid revenue growth alongside enormous losses: $1.8 billion revenue and a $1.9 billion net loss in 2018; about $1.54 billion revenue and a $900M+ net loss in the first half of 2019. The S-1 also disclosed governance and related-party red flags, including a $5.9 million payment to a Neumann-controlled entity for the 'We' trademark, leases of buildings owned by Neumann, low-interest loans to Neumann, and a dual-class structure giving him twenty votes per share. The combination of unprofitable growth and key-person governance risk undermined the IPO.
outcome_evidence: The S-1 disclosed a $1.9 billion net loss on $1.8 billion revenue for 2018 and a $900M+ loss for H1 2019, plus the $5.9 million 'We' trademark payment, Neumann building leases, loans, and 20-votes-per-share control. The IPO was subsequently shelved; Neumann later returned the $5.9 million and stepped down.
source_limitations: The SEC EDGAR S-1 document returned 403 to direct WebFetch in this environment, but the cited URL is the verified primary EDGAR filing location surfaced by search; all figures were confirmed verbatim across credible WebSearch snippets quoting the S-1 (CNBC, Fortune, Inc., Fox Business). H1-2019 net loss is stated as 'more than $900 million.'
directly_stated: 2018 net loss of $1.9 billion on $1.8 billion revenue
H1 2019: ~$1.54 billion revenue, >$900 million net loss
$5.9 million paid to a Neumann-controlled entity (We Holdings LLC) for the 'We' trademark
Neumann held twenty votes per share (dual-class control)
Company leased and paid rent on buildings owned by Neumann; extended low-interest loans to him
inferred: Core space-as-a-service unit economics did not scale to profitability despite revenue growth
Key-person governance concentration created enterprise-level risk that markets repriced
why_useful_for_opsiq: Rich multi-dimensional case combining unit_economics_failure (growth with hidden profitability problem) and key-person/governance risk. Tests whether a system models more than one dimension at once and does not treat fast revenue growth as evidence of health when losses and governance concentration are escalating.
